newsitem.title: JAPAN: Former copper star Hamanaka pleads guilty to fraud.
newsitem.headline: Former copper star Hamanaka pleads guilty to fraud.

text.p: Former Sumitomo copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka pleaded guilty to fraud and forgery at the start of his trial on Monday, admitting his role in a massive trading scandal that cost his employer $2.6 billion.

Dressed in a blue suit and white shirt but with no necktie, the once-powerful figure in the financial world admitted his guilt in a clear voice after the prosecution read through its case against him.
The charges carry a penalty of up to 15 years in prison.

Hamanaka, 49, who spent all of his professional life at trading house Sumitomo Corp, was considered the most powerful player in the global copper market, feared by other traders for the influence he wielded over the market.
He was fired last June by the company for what it said were years of unauthorised trading. Sumitomo estimates the improper trading cost the firm $2.6 billion.
Through his plea at Tokyo District Court, Hamanaka has avoided a lengthy hearing that might have answered many of the still-open issues in the Sumitomo copper scandal.
The criminal case does not cover the broader question of whether Hamanaka manipulated the world copper market and, if so, who benefited.
While those questions are being investigated by U.S. and British regulators, Japanese authorities say that since the copper deals all took place overseas, they are not involved.
The charges against Hamanaka were also narrowly drawn.
On the count of forgery, he admitted falsifying four letters in order to open accounts.

On the fraud count, he admitted to making an improper payment to Morgan Guaranty of New York, a subsidiary of banking firm J.P. Morgan and Co, after losing money on options in an account he held there.
The losses, totalling $771 million, were sent from the Hong Kong office of Sumitomo. Morgan Guaranty is not accused of any wrongdoing in the case.
The prosecution also said Hamanaka received a "gratitude payment" from Winchester Commodities, a London-based commodities trading group.

It was the first time that prosecutors had alleged that Hamanaka, known for his modest lifestyle despite his job as a "high-rolling" trader, had personally gained from his improper trading activities.
Even though Hamanaka entered guilty pleas, the hearing continued into the afternoon with a detailed reading of the case against him.
Reporters in the courtroom noticed that Hamanaka, who sat quietly after entering his pleas, was wearing green plastic sandals.
Like the Daiwa Bank scandal before it, the Sumitomo case has raised questions about Japan"s financial regulations.
In that case, a bond trader working in Daiwa Bank"s New York office was sentenced to four years in prison for hiding losses of $1.1 billion in unauthorised trades.
